title: 2025 Reconciliation Law Delays Provisions in Two Medicaid Eligibility Rules
description_short: 2025 Reconciliation Law Delays Provisions in Two Medicaid Eligibility Rules
description_medium: The 2025 reconciliation law delayed provisions in two Medicaid eligibility rules: the 2023 Medicare Savings Program rule and the 2024 Eligibility and Enrollment rule. KFF, citing CBO, projects the combined delay will save about $122 billion over ten years and increase the uninsured population by about 400,000 in 2034. The 1.3 million figure came from an earlier House-passed bill, not the enacted law.
description_long: The 2025 reconciliation law delayed until October 2034 parts of two Biden-era Medicaid and CHIP eligibility rules: the 2023 Medicare Savings Program rule and the 2024 Eligibility and Enrollment rule. The rules were intended to reduce administrative barriers to enrolling in and keeping coverage. KFF, citing Congressional Budget Office estimates, reported that delaying provisions in both rules would reduce federal spending by about $122 billion over 10 years and increase the uninsured population by roughly 400,000 in 2034. That estimate differs from an earlier 1.3 million figure for dual-eligible beneficiaries, which applied to the House-passed bill rather than the final law. The distinction matters because the legislation changed during negotiations and estimates tied to earlier versions should not be presented as final effects. The projected coverage changes are not counts of people already losing insurance; they describe a modeled future impact if the delayed rules do not take effect. The law’s delay may affect access and renewal processes for low-income beneficiaries.

supports: The enacted 2025 law delayed provisions in both the Medicare Savings Program and Eligibility and Enrollment rules.
KFF reports CBO projections of about $122 billion in combined federal savings and roughly 400,000 more people uninsured in 2034 for the two-rule delay.
limits: The combined estimate applies to the delay of both rules; it is not a precise observed count of people losing coverage or a projection attributable to only one rule.

supports: KFF’s earlier House-bill analysis reports the 1.3 million low-income Medicare/dual-eligible figure for a prior legislative version.
limits: This earlier House-bill estimate is not the final law’s precise effect.

source_access_notes: Both KFF pages were retrieved over HTTPS (HTTP 200). The final-law analysis distinguishes the combined two-rule projection from an earlier House-passed estimate; the earlier-version figure is retained only with that qualification.
unsupported_original_claims: The 1.3 million figure is not the enacted law’s precise projection for the two-rule delay.
The combined $122 billion projection is not attributable to the Eligibility and Enrollment rule alone.
remaining_evidence_gap: These sources report modeled coverage effects, not observed individual losses.
preservation_note: Only the medium description was shortened. The title, short description, long description, URLs, and supported claim scope are retained from the current proposal.

title: Trump FY2026 Budget Proposes Eliminating the Legal Services Corporation
description_short: Trump’s FY2026 budget sought to eliminate LSC and included $21 million for close-out costs
description_medium: The White House’s May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget proposal sought to eliminate the Legal Services Corporation and requested $21 million for close-out costs; LSC received $560 million in FY2025. Congress later enacted $540 million for FY2026 in Public Law 119-74. The February 2025 claim of completed defunding is inaccurate.
description_long: The Legal Services Corporation received a $560 million congressional appropriation for fiscal year 2025. In its May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget request, the Trump administration proposed eliminating LSC and requested $21 million for close-out costs. That request was a proposal, not a February 2025 cancellation of existing funding. Congress later enacted $540 million for LSC for FY2026 in Public Law 119-74, which specifies the amount and its program allocations. The enacted appropriation means the administration’s proposal did not become complete defunding. The supplied sources do not quantify any service reductions caused by the proposal or show that legal-aid offices immediately lost all federal support. This entry records the budget request, existing FY2025 appropriation, and later enacted FY2026 amount as distinct actions, without inferring that the proposal itself changed grants or ended services. The statute does not prove that no offices experienced disruption.

supports: LSC reported the May 30, 2025 FY2026 administration budget proposal to eliminate LSC and seek $21 million for close-out costs.
LSC reported a $560 million congressional appropriation in FY2025.
limits: The release describes a proposal; it does not show that the proposal was enacted or that services stopped.

supports: LSC’s official appropriations history distinguishes proposed budgets from enacted funding, records FY2025 funding continuity, and lists an FY2026 appropriation overview of $540 million.
limits: This is an appropriation-history page; it does not quantify service reductions resulting from the proposed budget.

supports: Public Law 119-74 is the enacted FY2026 legislation; its Legal Services Corporation payment provision appropriates $540,000,000.
limits: The law establishes the enacted appropriation, not service outcomes caused by the preceding budget proposal.

source_access_notes: The two LSC pages were retrieved over HTTPS (HTTP 200); the appropriations-history page explicitly lists the $540 million FY2026 overview. The GovInfo PDF returned HTTP 200; the same official package’s HTML rendition was checked and states a $540,000,000 LSC payment. All three retained source URLs are HTTPS.
unsupported_original_claims: The evidence does not support a February 2025 completed elimination of all LSC federal funding.
The May 2025 budget request was a proposal and did not itself cancel existing appropriations or grants.
The sources do not establish immediate cessation of services or quantify service reductions at legal-aid organizations.
remaining_evidence_gap: The sources do not quantify service reductions caused by the proposal or establish that no local provider experienced disruption.
preservation_note: All title and description text, the three current-proposal URLs, and the corrected scope are retained. The missing map is supplied for the existing LSC appropriations URL; no URL was removed or added.
